newsitem.title: USA: Florida judge to rule soon in assisted-suicide case.
newsitem.headline: Florida judge to rule soon in assisted-suicide case.

text.p: A judge on Thursday ruled that a 35-year-old Florida man who is dying from AIDS and may have less than a week to live can go ahead with a physician-assisted suicide.
Within an hour of the ruling, however, the state appealed and the case went to the Florida Supreme Court.

Circuit Judge Lucy Brown said there was no reason to keep Charles Hall from taking his life, adding that by the time the appeals were over Hall "will have been forced to suffer a miserable and degrading death."
Hall contracted AIDS after receiving a blood transfusion during treatment of Hepatitis B 13 years ago and since last January has been seeking court approval of his right to die.
Hall's doctor, Jupiter, Florida, physician Cecil McIver, said he thought his ailing patient might not survive the week.

In explaining the decision to push the case to the state's highest court assistant Attorney General Michael Gross said, "I believe there is a broader public policy issue to be decided as this case could affect the rights of all Florida residents."
Hall's attorney, Robert Rivas, objected, saying, "It appears the state is contining to play ping pong with Hall's life. It appears the state will stop at nothing in its harassment of Hall.
"Death is not a condition which can be reversed by any legal authority. There is no chance that a cure for AIDS will be found before he dies," Rivas said.
Hall was unable to leave his Beverly Hills, Florida, home as he battled AIDS-related pneumonia. He has refused treatment, saying it would not alter the course of the disease.

Last Friday Palm Beach County Judge Joseph Davis ruled Hall had the right to take his own life with the assistance of a doctor. But the state opposed Hall's action and announced it would appeal, triggering the stay.
Arguing for the state before the curcuit judge, assistant attorney-general Parker Thomson said Florida had a broader interest to protect the disabled, elderly and others from abuse.
"The state has a right to have these issues decided once and for all," Thomson said.
The no indication when the state's high court would rule on the issue.
